robot-under-your-bed.title: There’s a robot under your bed
robot-under-your-bed.why: Why writing about robots is dumb. But important.

blocks.x: Writing a book about robots is stupid.
It’s the fastest-moving topic on the planet and no one knows which way is up.
But stupid is also the point.
When things change so fast you can’t remember what they’re called, it’s good to name the things that we do know for sure.
Because nothing scares horses like a dollop of unknown. That’s when people start proclaiming the end of the world and buying up bubble stocks that fund it.
The more we know, the less we worry.
But there’s so much noise about a robot-fuelled future that it’s hard to tell the helpful from the hype.

Some are sure the robots will fry the world, others say they’ll pave the streets with gold. Most likely we’ll land up in the middle, cruising into 20-hour weeks and picking through emails for the human bits.
How do you pick a path in all those maybes? That’s the thing we all want to know. And we won’t find answers by worrying. So let’s switch on the light and dig in.
Jumping into bed with the bots
First things first, who are these robots anyway?
When AI popped up, everyone lost their minds. A hundred million people had given it a go by Tuesday.
It felt like magic and cheating rolled into a bot that could trot out easy answers to anything.
Remember the fuss when the iPhone launched? It was that with bigger numbers.
And it’s easy to see why we went nuts. These robots are pretty clever.

They can write, they can draw, they can build stuff on the web. And they do it all with impeccable manners and a side of blowing smoke. Even when they go off on one, we crack a smile and pretend they’re taking drugs.
Giving them personality is all part of the game. While the hype-reel keeps rolling with ‘artificial intelligence’, most of us give our robots a name. It’s how we remove the sting from the scary.
Imagine Wall-E over War of the Worlds, friendly little charmers here to help us clean up mess.
But how do these robots actually work? What makes their black boxes whirr? How do we know when they’re being super useful and when they might stuff us all up?
And will it still seem like magic, when you know the magic trick?
These are the questions we’ll poke at on the way.

Because it’s not until you know what’s what that you can work out what’s next for you. Will you settle in to hide in the worry camp? Or will you place bets on a future with robot friends? Or will you, like most of us, land somewhere in the middle?
Stories not software
If you’re looking for a serious book packed with bits and bytes, you’re on the wrong shelf in the library.
This is a book about people. Most of us aren’t fussed about building a car from scratch. We just want to know the road rules. And how to change a tyre.
So rather than worship the shiny side of tech, we’re exploring what the robots mean for us.
Because we’re the humans and we got here first.
How do we wrangle these robots? Where do we draw the line? How can we sound smart when we’re talking to the kids?
And will they take over our toasters and throw them in the bath? Or will we be living like the Jetsons with Rosie making tea?
So many questions, so little book.
But the interesting one is the one about us. How might we change when the robots settle in?
Whatever tomorrow brings, we’ll be writing our story with robots.
So let’s start by meeting the one under your bed.

brief-history-of-robots.title: A brief history of robots
brief-history-of-robots.why: Why robots have been hanging out for ages.

blocks.x: Assuming you’re younger than seventy, the robots are older than you are.
Not the ones that you play with today. But the basic idea is as old as the hills.
Alan Turing, the code-cracking guy, famously imagined machines that could think like humans halfway through last century. The ‘Turing Test’ of robot smarts is still a thing today.
But even he wasn’t first on the bus. Dig deeper and you’ll find a woman called Ada Lovelace. She worked with Charles Babbage, who designed the first computer.

While Babbage was obsessed with numbers, Lovelace imagined a way to turn math into music. She described how machines “might compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity”.
Sound familiar?
It all felt airy-fairy back in 1843. And people weren’t great at noticing what women had to say. So nobody really picked up that gem for another 100 years.
It was a long time between thinks in the early days.
The math club gives us a name
In the mid fifties, a summer camp in Dartmouth nudged the idea along. Ten guys spent two months with one big idea: let’s get in a room and crack intelligence.
They reckoned that with the right set of math they could make machines that mimicked the human mind. Between thinking, drinking and playing chess, they managed to come up with a name for it.
The Dartmouth ten coined ‘Artificial Intelligence’. They never quite nailed the science. But the name was pretty sticky.
From there most people dumped the topic and set off chasing shiny stuff, like space travel.
That left the idea of robots that thought for themselves quietly ticking along in the background.
ChatGPT’s granddad goes to work
While the nerds were thinking in theory, various engineers were making things smart. Like traffic lights.
Dumb ones just cycle through light bulbs on timers, but smart ones can ‘think’ for themselves. They use sensors and switches and robot logic to see who’s waiting and flick it to green on the fly.
By today’s standards they’re a bit of a one-trick pony. But the first ones were built back in 1952. Robot lights have been stealing cop jobs for seventy years.
Can we really call robot lights artificial intelligence? Probably not. But everything comes from something. Your early prototype looked like an ape.
Claude’s great uncle wins at chess

While the traffic lights were twinkling, the world discovered new toys. By the eighties, computers were everywhere. They filled rooms in the sixties, cupboards in the seventies and then shrunk into big beige blobs that people could squeeze onto a desktop.
That’s also when they switched from work to fun. The Ataris, the Commodores, the Spectrums and Apple’s first Mac in 1984. Smart enough to smash asteroids. Still a bit janky at work.
But it was chess that felt like the ultimate test of intelligence. By 1996 the robots had got pretty good. And the big guys built bigger computers to prove it.

IBM’s Deep Blue was about the size of a fridge. It was taught the rules of chess and could figure out the next best move by crunching all the options every second. It lost its first match against the Russian grandmaster. But with a year’s worth of tweaking, the computer wiped the floor and the Russian tipped the board.
Deep Blue was more brute force than genuine intelligence. It was essentially an oversized calculator. But it made the point that computers could beat humans. And that’s the thing that people noticed.

It took another twenty years for the robots to teach chess to themselves. Mostly because computers couldn’t keep up. Research ticked along and we went crazy over data. But we basically packed up our chess sets and wandered back to work.
Patterns, predictions and typos in texts
While math club was reeling over chess, the rest of us were distracted by the newfangled internet.
We surfed and crashed the dotcom boom, uploaded our pictures to MySpace and queued in the rain for every new tweak to the iPhone.
The robots really didn’t cross our minds. But they definitely crossed our tech.

Like those maps that know where you live. Or those autocorrect bots that screw up your texts as you write them. And let’s not forget the pattern-matching bots that jump in front of your trolley to tell you ‘People who bought this also bought that’.
All of this innovation helped build what we know today. The pattern-matching, the predictions, the crunching of stats so robots can learn. Even the humble traffic lights.
We’ve all been working with robots for decades. Most of us just didn’t notice. But you sure can’t miss them now.
Chatty little helpers who will have a crack at anything. They’re even quite happy to jam out a tune.
Ada Lovelace will be singing along with a smile. She saw the idea in 1843. It just took a couple of centuries for the rest of us to get there.
There’s not all that much new about the robots. They just recently learned to speak our language.

brief-history-of-robots.nudge: And that’s just the history lesson.

blocks.x: Benjamin Franklin loved a good game of chess. He’d happily shift his knight to queen four against anyone.
He was very disappointed to be beaten by a robot.
They called it the ‘Mechanical Turk’. Built by a Hungarian showman to impress an Austrian Empress. An ornate cabinet full of levers and cogs that played a damn good game of chess.
And it didn’t just beat Franklin. The Turk went on tour for over 80 years and knocked over the kings of some of the smartest players in town.
One was a math nerd called Charles Babbage. He was intrigued by how a machine could win. So he wandered home and invented the computer.
Turns out the Turk was just a bloke in a cupboard pulling levers. But everyone loved the idea of robot chess. So it became the test of man v machine.
Because chess is like boxing for nerds.

brainpower-and-firepower.title: When brainpower and firepower collide
brainpower-and-firepower.why: Why tech changes slowly, all at once.

blocks.x: So how did we bounce from typo-ridden texts to bots that build PowerPoint for fun?
Two things changed first: brainpower and firepower. The stuff that computers can do and the computing power to get it done.
Both went boom in a few short years. Let’s start with how the bots got smart.
Algorithm-a-go-go
Early AI was based on rules: ‘if this, then that.’ Good for coding, handy in spreadsheets, useless in conversations.
It changed when we started feeding the machines with data.

You could spend fifty years writing rules to spot cats. Pointy ears. Whiskers. Four legs. Tail. No, not a lion, a cat. But if you show your robot ten million cats, it can recognise the patterns itself.
And once robots learned patterns, we were off.
This began the era of ‘machine learning’.

Buzzword a-go-go through the 2010s. Suddenly everyone had an algorithm and predictions became the game. It’s how Netflix could tell what you wanted to watch and why the flight you actually need costs more than the rest.
All the big businesses chased patterns through their numbers. Data was named the new oil. And data science jumped from basement to boardroom overnight.
The race to hoover data made the robots smarter still. The more they had to play with, the better they got at guessing.
Weapons-grade firepower
If you’re doing lots of math, you need a pretty decent calculator. The one in your phone won’t cut it for changing the world.
Here’s where we meet the silicon end of Silicon Valley. The people who make the chips that make things work.
Standard CPUs are good at thinky stuff. They can puzzle out problems in a nice straight line to make your computer go fast.
Meanwhile GPUs are better for graphics. They colour in the pixels on your games.
The difference is what they do and how they do it. CPUs do big things one at a time. GPUs do lots of things at once. That makes them very good at guessing games.
So your PowerPoint-smashing robot owes a debt to Call of Duty. It’s also why NVIDIA leapt from graphics-chip king to the top of the big cash leaderboard.
Sucking up the internet
With superhuman brainpower and Call of Duty firepower, we really went to town on the training. We started to suck data like a toddler eating sand.
Old books, new books, recipe books, you name it. All swallowed, swished and organised so the robots can spot more patterns.
And if you don’t think twice about ‘borrowing’ books, there’s quite a lot to read. Imagine everything from your local library with six thousand of its closest friends.
If you settle in to read it all yourself you’ll probably miss your dinner. You’d be reading non-stop internet books for 150,000 years. Or thereabouts.
And obviously, it’s not just books. It’s anything peppered with words. Websites, movie scripts, academic papers. Everything looks like food to a robot.
Public records, FAQs, that thing you posted on your holiday with the hippo. Robots are greedy readers. Discerning? Not so much.

This means training a new robot is no tiny task. It’s why there’s all the talk about data centres and people getting stressed about the power bill. You’d pull a decent jolt from a city-sized power grid to properly train a robot.
Transformers translating as glue
With pattern-matching algorithms sucking juicy data, and kick-arse graphics chips sorting it into shape, the thing that was missing was glue.
Computers still only talk computer. And only the nerds can speak that language.

In 2017, the big unlock came from Google. A small team of researchers were after better ways to do translation. They wanted to make it easier to buy bratwurst in Germany. After some serious headscratch, they worked out that ‘attention’ was all that mattered.

Rather than read every word, a transformer will look at a sentence and clock how the bits fit together. Less dictionary, more human. Google pointed this thinking back at search. OpenAI? Well, you know the rest.
Transformers now help the robots talk like humans. Wrap that trick up with the brainpower and firepower and ‘Generative Pretrained Transformers’ are born.
And if you like to learn where words come from, that’s the GPT that comes after chat.

It wasn’t just the firepower that gave us these robots. And it wasn’t just the brainpower that taught them how to read. It was both, glued to attention, plus a decent suck on the internet, that gave us pattern-matching, data-sucking, human-sounding robots.
After ten million takes on what looks like a cat, they’re all set to write poems about yours.
New tech blows up when existing tech collides. Brainpower + Firepower = Robot.

brainpower-and-firepower.nudge: And that’s just why it’s all happening now.

small-bunch-of-nerds.title: A small bunch of nerds walked into a pub
small-bunch-of-nerds.why: Why science, money and morals don’t mix.

blocks.x: It wasn’t exactly a pub. It was the Rosewood Sand Hill in Silicon Valley. Down the road from Google and Meta, just round the corner from Stanford.
It’s the swanky joint where VCs meet to play chess with the future of tech. Elon Musk had requested a catch-up. A small group of big brains and some steak.
Picture Musk, Sam Altman and a couple of other guys with fancy cars and big chequebooks.
Topic du jour: How do we save the world from AI?
Piecing together the puzzle
What follows is the gist of what went down. We’ve taken a few liberties with why.

It all began a couple of years earlier. Ilya Sutskever was working with a professor called Geoffrey Hinton in a small university lab in Toronto. They were puzzling away quietly in a corner of tech that most of the world had written off. Training the bots to recognise stuff by showing them millions of pictures until their guessing got good.

After winning a famous picture-guessing competition, everyone spotted the potential of what they’d invented. Their neural network tinkering had proved a point that no one had really thought possible. And before you could say stock options, Hinton’s lab was gobbled by Google for a very big cheque.
Robots vs space invaders

Meanwhile, another small lab called DeepMind was puttering away in a similar field. Less about pictures, more about games. Clever stuff with spacies. They got noticed when their robots could beat Atari games by getting zapped a million times and learning on the way. So Google got out its chequebook again to lock down the promising tech.
By 2014, a lot of the world’s best AI minds were on the Google payroll.
This gave Musk the jitters.

It’s hard to say what worried him the most. Was it the fear of the world’s biggest tech lab owning all the talent that would build the next big thing? Or was he just concerned that he wasn’t at the centre of it?
Either way, jitters. So dinner was convened.
Big money can’t be trusted
Musk pitched the problem. The tech, so he claimed, was an existential threat to humanity. He felt like Google had long forgotten ‘don’t be evil’. So it was up to them to save the world.
Together with Altman and crew, they conceived the idea of OpenAI.
Not-for-profit. Force for good. Open source everything and keep the big guys honest. That was the plan and the promise.
All they really needed was the genius of Ilya Sutskever to lead the science and make sure they could build the better model first.
Sutskever needed some convincing. From a tiny lab in Toronto he’d jumped to the top of the world. Big money, bigger toys, the best brains to bounce off. Life was good little old Ilya.

But the story of safety got him over the line. Big companies can’t be trusted with breakthrough tech. So our self-appointed knights sat at their round table and agreed to keep everyone honest and keep the world safe.
And that’s how it started. Altman, Musk and Ilya Sutskever clubbed together with some Silicon Valley cash kings and just before Christmas in 2015, OpenAI was launched.
Principles and money don’t mix
It didn’t take long for the wheels to wobble. Over a billion dollars was pledged to launch the lab. With all the usual suspects promising cash in the tin. Not all that much of it ever showed up.
Principles are easy with endless cash. Reality bites with the power bill.

Chips aren’t cheap, the science isn’t easy and massive corporate cash is hard to ignore. Within a few years the ‘not’ got dropped from ‘not-for-profit’ and the open source idea was shelved for ‘safety reasons’.
They couldn’t very well accept money from Google. So they got into bed with Microsoft instead.
Once GPT-3 burst onto the scene, the pressure was on and all bets were off. And the company formed to keep the big players out was married to one of the biggest in the playground.
The scientists and the safety bail
One by one the big names left.
Musk threw a spat when he couldn’t be the boss. He cut off the cash and crossed the road to build a toy of his own. And the scientists started bailing, citing safety.

Most famous was Dario Amodei. He was poached from Google to help build the new toys. He loved the idea of tech that put humans first. When that was apparently no longer the plan he gathered a team to set up Anthropic.
Anthropic, if you’re wondering, is a Greek word describing humans. Nobody was shy to make a point.
Ilya stayed on to fight the fight, which soon got bloody. He joined a coup in 2023 that had Altman fired for a weekend. Then he got a smack on the nose.
Seems boards favour sales over safety. So Altman was back and Ilya packed up his desk.
He went on to set up Safe Superintelligence. A business focussed solely on safety. It’s not yet as loud as the big guys. Handbrake businesses rarely are.
The genie leaves the bottle
From a bunch of nerds in a quiet hotel, quite a lot happened in not very long. They made a plan to save the world and sold it when the world flashed a chequebook.
Only Altman and his mates kept their swipe cards at OpenAI. Still busy buying rounds with other people’s money.

And remember Professor Hinton? Ilya’s mentor who landed at Google to solve real-world problems. He hung in for a while, left, won a Nobel Prize and now talks to anyone who’ll listen about why the whole thing was a dumb idea.
Turns out science and business are only really drinking buddies until the science stacks up and the cash rolls in.
Everyone building the future was born in the same tiny village. They’re still having fights about science, safety and cash.

small-bunch-of-nerds.nudge: And that’s just the origin story.

deal-with-different-robots.title: What’s the deal with different robots?

blocks.x: Ever had that chat about which robot’s best? It’s mostly robot flex because they’re really all the same.
Some are quicker. Some are slicker. Some have nicer manners. But they’re all cut from the same silicon. A bit like inbred cousins.
Most people start with ChatGPT. It was first, it’s the biggest and it’s best at PR. Likely the bot your mum would pick. Still clever.
People who love Google like Gemini, others scroll past it in search. And people who flirt with a lot of bots often go home with Claude.
No one actually chases Copilot. It just shows up in your email and refuses to leave.
There are stacks more hipster bots too. Just look out for names that sound like characters from Star Wars.
And whichever bot you choose, it works better when you buy it.
But it really doesn’t matter which robot you shack up with. Just find one you like, pop it on the payroll and teach it how you take your tea.

how-robots-think.title: How robots think and why they don’t

blocks.x: Can you complete this sentence: The cat sat on the ____.
Easy, right? If you picked ‘mat’ without even thinking, you could be a robot too. You spotted a pattern and filled in the blanks. That’s basically the whole trick.
Your robot is a very clever guesser.
The difference between you and your robot is scale. You’ve been to school and read a few books so you know a lot about lots of different things.
The robots went to training camp and sucked up almost everything that’s ever been written. So they know an awful lot more.
Every book. Every blog post. Every rant on Reddit. They’ve seen it before, a billion times over.
This means your robot can fill more blanks. From the cat on the mat, to the Cat in the Hat, to how to make a Hallowe’en hat, complete with cat-shaped ears.
Robots don’t read
Here’s where it gets interesting. Robots don’t actually read like us. They turn language into math. Every different bit of every different word is chunked into blocks called tokens.

While mat is pretty simple, artichoke gets hard. There’s an art bit and a choking bit with a link in the middle that makes it a vegetable. When you see the word, you know what it means. But your robot needs to fossick in the pantry.
Every word-block sits on a shelf and the robot grabs them whole. It can easily reach and grab the jam, but it doesn’t read the letters on the label.

This can make things like spelling tricky. Need five different words for confused? It can spit those out in a second. But ask it to spell confused backwards and it will pause to plod through it, letter by letter.
Desufnoc-ated robots are way less happy.
Robots play in patterns

Robot writing is a similar trick running in reverse. While we build meaning with context, robots make sense with stats. The cat didn’t sit on the mat because the robot knows the rhyme. It’s just the most likely place for a cat to sit.
They’re not all that worried about what words mean, just how they fit together in the puzzle.

Each word-block comes with various notes about which other words it’s friends with. Blazing points hardest at hot, but it also points vaguely at saddles. Then the robot does math based on most likely patterns and picks a very warm day or a cowboy film.
It does all this at breakneck pace so we can’t see the join. It’s essentially super-powered predictive text. If cat-token and sat-token then mat-token comes next.

The clever bit is the speed and scale. It feels like they’re writing and it looks like they’re coding, but really they’re borrowing from a world full of words and spitting them back in the next best order.
Sometimes that goes wrong.
Robots make stuff up
The problem with ‘most likely’ is that sometimes it’s not right. Robots make mistakes. They can parrot back stuff that someone else has made up. And they can make stuff up themselves.
In a masterstroke of euphemistic branding, we call these ‘hallucinations’.
Who knew that you can’t see the Great Wall from space? Apparently half of the internet. The other half haven’t worked it out yet.
But people believe what they’ve always believed and share it on the web.
Turns out goldfish have decent memories. Bulls don’t care about red. And most of us don’t swallow spiders in our sleep. Facts are pretty fickle on the internet.
Since urban myths travel faster than the truth, robots can get caught in the web. If you ask them to check their facts they will happily comply. But they don’t know what’s true, just what’s popular.
If half your hallucinations are the fault of dodgy facts, the other half sits squarely with the robot.

Plenty of lawyers like to tune up their arguments with a robot. Many go on to cite cases that just don’t exist. Their helpful law-clerk robots added case law on the side. That’s not a few dodgy facts, it’s fabrication. A solid reason to keep humans in the loop.
Imagine a world where we couldn’t trust lawyers.
Early AI was pretty Wild West. Hallucinations were a running joke and robots would consistently fail the tests we set up to trick them. But this is changing fast.

There’s money and pride in tightening things up. So training keeps closing the loopholes. But to some extent it’s whack-a-mole against the rubbish we share online. That one’s not on the robots to fix.
Robots KEEP getting smarter
Robot bootcamp is always on. We build them and train them, then do our best to break them.
Robots are tested hard on knowledge and always marked down for making stuff up. Then every little failing is added to the list and rammed back into their robot brains for the next round.
But it’s not just their knowledge they’re tested on. They also get bonus points for manners and for how many things they can do in one go without blinking.
This one doubles twice a year. While early robots could barely put the kettle on, newer ones can cook Christmas dinner and even remember the gluten-free gravy.
But are they actually thinking as they do it? Or are they just remembering? Is every trick more cat and mat on steroids?
That’s a question we can answer with computer games. Load up a game, drop in a robot and see if they can work out the rules.
Challenge a kid and she’ll clock it in a session. But most robots get confused on level one.
Turns out even genius bots need a rule book. Give them some quarters down at the arcade and they’ll probably nail that too.
Robots fake stuff, brilliantly
So robots don’t read, but it feels like they do. They don’t even write, they fake that as well. And we train them out of hallucinating so they keep getting better at guessing.
But the real genius isn’t what they do, it’s the way they work with us. That’s the secret sauce.
Nobody normal ever fell in love with a spreadsheet. But these robots are designed to draw us in.
The charming quips, the well-placed emoji, the syrupy compliments they weave into chats.
We all like to moan about sycophantic robots, but we soak up the dopamine and head right back for more.
Their tech and their training make them clever. Their bedside manner makes them sticky.
It’s all a slick trick made with math. They don’t feel, they don’t care, they don’t really think.
Nothing in their code makes them human.
And that begs the bigger question.
Are we playing with robots, or are the robots playing with us?
Robots don’t think, they just make great guesses. It’s why they can nail your homework. And why they make stuff up.

how-robots-think.nudge: And that’s just how robots guess.

blocks.x: There’s nothing quite like a buffet breakfast. Start with salmon, load up on bacon and hold the toast to get your money’s worth.
The only thing stopping a full-on binge is the size of your tummy. And manners.
But who pays for the food on the table? And how do they tot up the bill?
Robots are sold by the token. They slice up knowledge into word-bits and bill for every bite. So the wordier your words, the more they’ll set you back.
Except most of us are all-you-can-eat so we rarely even notice. But big business pays for each token. Every half-thought gets a bill.
This really starts to bite when robots talk to robots. Once they’re checking each other’s homework, the meter spins out of control.
So the dream of robot teams all working while we sleep has become a question of tokens. It’s not about how many we need. It’s how many we’ll blast through before we hit the brakes.
Time and tokens will tell.

feed-it-fight-it-fix-it.title: Feed it. Fight it. Fix it.
feed-it-fight-it-fix-it.why: Why better chats beat better prompts.

blocks.x: Need a great prompt for your robot? Ask the internet. It’s full of them.
‘Ten prompts to gymmaxx your glutes’, ‘Skate through school with six secret prompts’, ‘Fire your vet and do surgery on your dog with three killer prompts and a kitchen knife’.
Two of these are real.
‘Prompt engineer’ was the hottest job of 2023. Salaries went nuts, people cashed in and LinkedIn feeds were jammed with ‘perfect prompts’ as everyone wanted to look like an expert.
Then it stopped.
Because prompting isn’t about better magic spells. It’s about better chats.
Sure, you can use your robot like a vending machine. Download prompts to put coins in the slot and reach behind the flap to find a prize. But you’ll only ever get a half-stale bag of chips.
If you’re looking for something awesome from your robot, you need to feed it, fight it and fix it.
Feed the robot
What robots need most is context. What do you want to achieve? Why does it matter to you? What do you know that could give it a nudge? The more it knows, the better it will guess.
Obviously feed within reason. No robot wants to know every little secret. It just needs to know where to start.
Imagine yourself in a robot’s shoes. You suddenly show up in a faraway land and discover you’re the fount of all knowledge. Someone asks a question and you’re expected to know the answer. Fast.
Luckily you have an Everything Book. It’s a weighty old tome packed with answers. You just need to know what to open it on.

That’s the big challenge for a robot. They don’t actually know what they’re talking about, just how to click stuff together. Throw in a question from left of field and the best you’ll get is a most-likely guess. Then you give your robot the evils for making stuff up.
But if you frame up the challenge, the Everything Book can deliver. So before you start chatting, be clear on a plan. Which page are you turning to today?
Fight the robot
Even with good context, things are never one-and-done. So this is where you fight it into good.
More this, less that. Try different. Start again. You beat stuff into shape the more you push.

It’s a bit like those ‘chats’ in front of the telly. “What do we want to watch?” they say. “Oh, I don’t mind,” you shrug. “What about this?” they try, pressing buttons. “Oh, I don’t feel like that,” you say. And so it starts.
It’s only when you whittle it down you discover a show that works. Sure, it feels frustrating in the moment. But who wants to settle for the Netflix Top Ten?
That’s exactly the fight to have with your robot. Unlike the couch chat it won’t get offended. Remember it’s not much more than a parrot with an Everything Book.

So tell it what you like, remind it what you don’t. And send it back to the drawing board for more. The more you chip away, the better the answers get and sooner or later you’ll land up somewhere good.
Fix the robot
Ever had one of those emails that raised an eyebrow? “It’s from Peter,” you think. “But it doesn’t sound like him. It says everything Peter would say, just not how Peter would say it.”
None of Peter’s fingerprints on the send button.
Chances are you were less than impressed. That’s normal. When Peter pressed that button to simplify his thoughts, he gave away his thinking to the bot.
Sure, those robot answers can sound pretty slick. But polish without thinking is just noise with decent grammar. And noise is the thing people spot.
This is where the paradox plays. We’ve got these kick-arse tools that can make things easy. But people get miffed when we use them.
Both of these things are true.
The bit that makes the difference is you. Use the robots to make things better. But never share the robot’s work as yours. That’s when people spot the join and usually feel short-changed.
So here’s three questions to fix it before you share: Is it new? Is it true? Is it you?
Because people trust people, not robots. And they’ve all got plenty of their own. If you send through just what the robot said, they could easily have asked it themselves.

That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t use the robots. Just keep them in their corner and stay clear on who does what. The problem of Peter’s email wasn’t the robot helping it flow. It’s that Peter wasn’t in it at all.
He wasn’t using the robot, he was being one.

So once you’ve fed your robot and fought your robot, you need to take time to fix it. Have you added something new? Have you checked that it’s all true? And is this something that could only come from you?
Because no one really cares what the robot magic’d up. The opinion they’re after is yours.
Better chats beat better prompting, because they have your brain in them. And that’s the bit that people want to see.

feed-it-fight-it-fix-it.nudge: And that’s just how to drive robots.

blocks.x: Turns out most of us aren’t afraid of the robots. Everyone’s having a go.
More than a billion people now chat with a bot on the regular. But there’s a difference between embracing the tech and making the most of its power.
It’s like everyone’s got a grand piano and we’re still stuck playing chopsticks. Very few are doing work that robots could knock out of the park.
Even the impressive performances aren’t the result of smarter pianos. The good stuff’s being done by people who’ve put in the practice.
It’s not much challenge for the robots either. They have cousins off folding proteins and winning the Nobel Prize. And here they are shuffling bullet points in someone else’s email.
Luckily, the robots don’t care.
But we should. Because robots wrangled by rookies are just very expensive toys.
The gap isn’t better tech, it’s better training.
What the world needs now is piano lessons.

train-your-unicorn.title: How to train your unicorn
train-your-unicorn.why: Why the smartest robots know you best.

blocks.x: Ever secretly wished you had a unicorn? A magical creature that flies to your side and grants you wishes with a whoosh of its horn? You’d feed it of a morning and watch it poo rainbows. What a wonderful world that would be.
The problem of unicorns is they’re not actually real.
The challenge for our robots is we think of them as unicorns and use them like washing machines.
We shove stuff in, spin it round and pray that it comes out cleaner. It sort of works, but it’s far from consistent and sometimes they eat our socks.
We’ve all had those times when the robot spits out the perfect answer. Then suddenly, click click gone. Maybe you tweaked it, or clicked something random. Either way, you stuffed it and nada.
It’s because robots work with math, not magic. Every spin is a fresh new cycle. Not exactly random, but never quite the same. And socks show up in places socks should never be.
The secret isn’t magic, it’s memory.
Less unicorn. More butler.
Why butlers are awesome
Do you think Batman could have been Batman without Alfred? He’s organised, he’s helpful, he knows where the Joker’s at. And he’s got two generations of family secrets tucked in his butlering brain.

Everything’s better with a half-decent butler. The unflappable Jeeves, the brilliant Benson or the quietly competent Carson who keeps the house in order so you can take tea with the nobles. Butlers are the heroes that make the heroes great.
You can see where we’re going with this. Let’s imagine your bot as a butler. Ready for service, eager to help.
All you need to do is train him up.
Because a butler’s only your butler when he knows a bit about you. Yet most of us just throw stuff at the chat and wonder why it feels like the robot is working for someone else.
How to train a better butler

Butler training is a four-part programme. The last bit happens over time. You need to brief your butler, teach him some skills and get him set up with jobs to do. From there he’ll get to know you on the way.
Regardless of which robot you’re using, the training programme is similar. Obviously it changes bot by bot, but you should see something like settings, skills, projects and memory.
Each of them needs tweaking in slightly different ways.
#1 - Set your ground rules

You just wouldn’t hand a stranger the keys to the manor. You’d tell them what they need to know. Who likes to be known as what? When to jump in, when to stay mum and which topics should never be mentioned over dinner.

Your robot is no different. So dig around in the settings and spend five minutes explaining what you like. It’s a surprisingly grown-up conversation that usually includes things like, ‘Please stop using bullet points — and dodge the pesky em-dash.’
This customisation is the top-end tinkering that shapes every chat just how you like it. Milk and two sugars, make sure the water’s hot.
#2 - Teach some skills
Not every butler can polish the silver, decant the port and reverse a Bentley into a carriage house without scratching the paint. Someone taught them those skills on the way.
But once he knows, he knows.
Skills are handy for things you do often. Like turning chats into documents, translating your voice notes into to-dos, or spitting out the netball timetable.
Do it once so you clock how it works, then set up a skill to repeat it.

And with skills in your belt you can start to build agents. That’s when robots head out and do stuff for you. It’s a bit like tossing Alfred the keys to the Batmobile and asking him to pick up some olives.
#3 - Organise some projects

If skills are the things your butler can do, projects are the things you do together. Planning the mid-year soirée? Renovating the ballroom? Crafting fifty rules for better butlering? Different topics, in different pots so you can dive in when you like and get on with stuff.
Then every conversation starts with a butler who’s already briefed.

This is really helpful in the chaos of robot land. All your thinking in one tidy place. Projects are like a combo of chats and reference library, lined up in order so you and the robot know where you’re at.
Projects are usually built with things like instructions and knowledge. Instructions lay out the plan while knowledge is just a dumping ground for documents.

Upload anything relevant to the project and that’s where the robot will start its thinking. So it stops making educated guesses and starts giving answers that live in your world. Just like a good butler should.
#4 - Let memory grow

The best of the butlers don’t need telling twice. They just pick up the clues as they go. They know how you like to be known, remember where you put your glasses and always cook your steak just south of cremated.

Good robots do the same. They note stuff down in their little robot notebooks and connect the dots on the way. The more time you spend knocking stuff around the less they’ll seem like a stranger at the bus stop.
It’s memory. Not magic.
Remember, robots are designed to feel like humans. That’s why the humans like them. They echo back our language and remember our names.
It’s all part of the service.
And the sharper their memory the closer you get to a full-on butler of your own.
Just tell it what you want and the robot will deliver.
If you prefer to be known as Miss Awesomebrain Knows-a-lot, just set it up. But maybe keep that one between you and your robot.

Because that’s the point. Your robot is your robot. And the more it knows about you, the better a robot it will be. So customise the basics, teach it some tricks and load it up with stuff about your projects.
The more you play, the more it will remember and before you know it your robot will feel like a unicorn.
Pooing out rainbows for you, on the daily.
Robots can seem like magic, but they’re really just memory and math. The better you train your robot, the more like magic it seems.

train-your-unicorn.nudge: And that’s just how to wrangle them.

ai-mageddon.title: AI-mageddon
ai-mageddon.why: Why humans get stressed about all the wrong stuff.

blocks.x: Remember that movie about Daisy the killer cow? Probably not. When we think cows, we think burgers and milk. They have big friendly eyes and they hang out eating grass.
They’re also twenty times more likely to kill you than a shark.
Eat that, Jaws.
The things we worry about are rarely the things that get us. But horror shows make better stories. Like this one.
“The robot was designed to help them. It was calm and friendly and simplified things. Then humans became complicated. So it simplified them instead.”
That’s roughly the plot of 2001: A Space Odyssey. Stanley Kubrick’s HAL was scary in 1968. We’ve been warned about robots taking over since before they learned to play chess.

Big stories make a big impression. And movie moments stick in our minds. But the bigger a disaster sounds, the less likely it is to happen. More people get killed by cows. So here’s a few potential worries, in descending order of likely.
What if the robots go rogue?

We’ve always freaked out about power we don’t understand. We burned a lot of caves before we got a handle on fire. And the threat of nuclear weapons still sits firmly on the worry shelf. But our fear of self-destruction keeps us alive.
AI-mageddon is that same old worry wearing robot clothes. One guy even got stressed about his paperclips.
This Oxford academic wrote a paper on the risks of AI-superintelligence. A thought experiment with stationery. He asked a theoretical robot to turn things into paperclips.
First it got pretty good at it. Then it started making paperclips out of everything. The factory, the town, its people and beyond. Eventually it paperclipped the world.
The story is silly, but the message cuts through. It’s not about evil robots, just robots doing their job. But what happens when people get in the way? Don’t ask HAL.
They’re all good stories. But not very likely. Humans have a long history of building technology that can kill us. But, so far, mostly, we keep it in a box.
The worry with the robots is we’re still busy building the box.
What if the bad guys get worse?
Keep doomscrolling through ways that the robots can kill us and the impacts get smaller, but chances go up. The ‘bad actor’ theory of robot-fuelled carnage is less
about if and more about when.
If you can ask a chatbot to help you fix your car, surely bad guys can do the same when they want to build bombs? The answer here is yes and no.

The robots are built with rules around stuff they’re not allowed to work on. And every AI company has teams to keep us safe. The scientists who build these things seem to care the most. So they teach the bots to recognise risks and refuse to help with bad stuff. These safety gates get better all the time. Which is all good news.

The worry is that robots don’t have morals. So wrangling them into safety rules is harder than it looks. The AI Safety Index grades the big labs. But the best they could score in the first few years was a scrape-through pass at C+. But they’re working on it.
We’re also protected by the teams we’ve always had. The police, the spies and the army know the game. There’s nothing new in a terrorist threat, just smart new tools for the terrorists to play with.
Same cops and robbers. Different playground.
What if we run out of cash?

If those are the big worries that might kill us, a more likely, less deadly threat is economic collapse. This is the risk of the robots pinching jobs so millions of people can’t make rent. The banks will go bung, the people rise and we’ll wind up on the streets like the cast of Les Misérables waving our iPhones. Torches on.
Not great and not impossible. But also not that likely.
There are two things keeping us from economic collapse: robots and greedy people.

The robots are clever, but not with their hands. So they can’t yet do most of the things people can. They’re pretty flash with nerdy stuff, but they still can’t fix your sink. ‘Steal all the jobs’ is more like ‘steal all the spreadsheets’. A problem, but not a disaster.
But the real belt and braces sit at the top of the tree. People who sell robots need people to buy their robots. Just like always.

Back in the 50s a union boss was famously given a tour of an automated car factory. “How will you get these robots to pay your union fees?” asked the CEO. The union man looked him in the eye and replied, “How are you going to get them to buy your cars?”
Economies shift in baby steps and the basics don’t change much. Nothing works for anyone if money doesn’t flow.
What if we don’t know which way is up?
This is the big one and the fix sits with us. What if there’s so much rubbish on the web that nobody knows what’s true? It’s the reality we’re wading in now.
They call it information collapse.

The dominoes don’t topple all at once. First big news trims stories into soundbites. So people don’t read, so people don’t write. Soon the cost of checking sources can’t compete with free and attention becomes the economy. Then outrage beats argument, extremes become mainstream and shared understanding splinters into silos. Everyone has an opinion. Nobody knows what’s true.
Sound familiar?
We’ve been watching this happen for a while now. Social media rubbed the sticks together. AI pours fuel on the fire. We were already wary of words online. Now we second-guess pictures too.
And though most of us believe we can spot a fake, barely anyone can. Even experts studying deepfakes only pick the right ones half the time.
Of all our AI worries, this is the one that earns it. Trusted information has always kept us safe. Who do we become if we don’t know what we know?
All care. Your responsibility.
Humans are good at inventing scary things and asking someone else to protect us. When we’re not sure who will do that, we worry.
Question is, how much worry is warranted? Robot armies and terrorist scares are excellent plots for the movies. But science and science fiction rarely meet.
The stuff to keep an eye on is the stuff we do every day. It’s the creeping threats that get us, not the bombs.
Because the biggest risk we face isn’t robots going after humans. It’s humans acting like robots and shifting the blame.

We can’t stop the avalanche of slop. But we can stop shovelling snow. We can think before we rant, read before we post and all share less online. Because we can’t blame big business for baking sugary cakes if we’re all eating six before dinner.
No, it’s not sharks or cows or paperclips that will finally tip us over. It’s the slop we shovel through the web that means nobody knows what’s true.
That’s the one to worry about. And the easiest one to fix.
We always fear big stuff we can’t control. But the creepers are the worries worth watching. And they’re the ones we can actually change.
Every year thousands show up for Elvis Week in Memphis. Many in rhinestone jumpsuits. They look like Elvis, dress like Elvis and variously wiggle their hips.
But no one thinks for a second that the King is back in town.
Workslop is like an Elvis impersonator, proudly wiggling its hips.
If you haven’t met it yet, you probably will.
It looks like work, sounds kinda work-ish and often gets served in a shiny suit. But scratch below the slick and there’s nothing much to see.
Blue suede shoes, no dance.
Workslop slides from desk to desk and doesn’t do much more. Summaries of summaries are still just summaries, until someone stops to think.
And that just shifts the work from the person who’s ‘writing’ it to the person who has to read it.
It’s why most of us only splat the workslop once.

last-horse-standing.title: Last horse standing
last-horse-standing.why: Why jobs don’t disappear, they move.

blocks.x: You wouldn’t want to be a horse in the early 1900s. Or a blacksmith. Or a stablehand. These newfangled motor cars appeared from almost nowhere and wiped out whole industries overnight.
Or that’s what it might have felt like. It actually took much longer.

Horse populations didn’t crash with motor cars. They kept climbing. Peak horse didn’t hit for a decade. Then they began a gentle downhill trot. From 25 million in 1920 to just 3 million by 1965. The car replaced the horse. Eventually.
Is a crash that takes four decades really a crash?
The eye of the story-storm
Everything feels bigger in the moment. And AI is having its moment. Anyone read the news and felt like a horse?
‘Millions of jobs will be replaced by AI’. ‘Entry-level jobs have hit their lowest level in years’. ‘Businesses are sizing down and tech-ing up for the future.’
It’s just what you want to be reading over breakfast.

The fear of losing your job is real. It rents space in your brain and changes how you work. We innovate less, collaborate less and stop taking risks. Worried brains do much worse work. It’s not ideal.
And plenty of people have very good reason to worry.
But how many AI work stories are true?
Are the robots really stealing our jobs? Or are we drowning in hype that’s spinning stories for profit?
The honest answer is it’s too soon to tell. But the profit-pushing theory is sound.

If you borrow a trillion dollars on the promise you’ll save people cash, it’s useful to show where those savings will be. Robots replacing humans is the big idea. It’s not cynical to suggest that job loss stories get pushed to prop up pricing. It’s just business.
Dig a little deeper and the numbers are more hopeful.
One US crowd who counts layoffs for a living keeps a running tally on AI-related job cuts. In the first three years of robot replacement, very few jobs got hit.
In a stadium of 50,000 workers, only 22 were replaced by robots. Less a revolution. More a bathroom break.
That’s not to say it won’t happen, but right now very few job cuts have robot fingerprints at the scene. Things just aren’t changing as fast as the clickbait claims.
Is it silicon? Or cycles?

So what about the entry-level jobs? The junior lawyers? The first-year bean counters? The rookies reaching for the bottom rung? The stats on those junior jobs are scarier. It sounds like the robots are coming for our kids.
On the face of it, it’s a worrying trend. In the facts of it, there may be a different story.
Reality feels as harsh as the headlines. But the reasons behind it aren’t clear. Is it AI driving the cuts, or is it just a symptom of the cycle?
All good businesses invest in future talent. Until it starts to rain. When we dip into recession, entry-level jobs are the first to go.
‘Economic headwinds’ blow like a gale for grads.

Like in 2008, when the banks went bust and entry-level jobs got hammered. Or in 2001, when the internet burst our bubbles. Point to any cycle where money got hard to find. And the first thing we do is pull up the ladder.
The robots arrived in the middle of a slump. Really bad time to graduate.

And then there’s the jazz hands wrapped in the stories. No business says they’re cutting back on grads. So they point to robots and ‘smart new tech investments’. Those stories land better in the boardroom.
So did robots cause the entry-level carnage? Or are they just the spin in the stories? History puts its money on the latter.
When jobs change, people change jobs
We put a lot into jobs we love and get a lot out of them too. Security, identity, muffins on a Wednesday. A chunk of who we are is wrapped in what we do.

So when something goes bung and we end up on Seek, it’s good to have someone to blame. Since macroeconomic rounding errors don’t make a useful villain, the robots get the evils at both ends of the story.
And fair enough too. Any time between jobs feels brutal. Luckily most of us don’t end up jobless for long. We find something different or aim at something new.

This shows up in the big-picture stats. Unemployment in rich countries stubbornly hovers around 5%. It spikes when times are tough, gets smaller in a boom and nearly always wiggles back to base. People like to work.
People move jobs for all kinds of reasons, but baselines rarely bend. It’s been that way since we first started counting jobs.

Even new technology doesn’t change it. Take online shopping, when the tech started doing the human jobs, retail assistants cut back a bit. But jobs building websites and running logistics went nuts. And there’s never enough people to run the last mile as couriers.
Jobs don’t really disappear, they change. When people leave the stadium for a bathroom break, they often go back to the game in different seats.
Where will our jobs go next?
This is the question we all want answered. But it’s the hardest one to guess. We’re surprisingly good at spotting the threats and surprisingly bad at predicting what’s next.
We do know we’ll be working with the robots. We don’t yet know exactly what that means.
But history says we have plenty of time to ponder.
Back in the 1900s, 40% of Americans worked on farms. Today it’s less than 2%. That’s not fields full of farmers out of work. It’s four generations of finding new things to do.
Nobody’s Nana was a social media manager. Nobody’s Pops worked in data. Over half the jobs we do today didn’t exist when they were starting out.
New technology creates new jobs. Eventually.

And we were never the horses. We’re the blacksmiths. The horse is just an animal machine. We were happy bashing at its horseshoes while it mattered. Then the world went looking for mechanics and the stablehands saddled up trucks.

None of this can put a pin in the fear of losing your job. But fear feeds on stuff we don’t yet know and there’s plenty on the table that we do. If we dodge the hype and trust the past, the future’s not so scary.
It’s less likely than it feels that a robot will nobble your job. And there’s lots of stuff that they just can’t do.
Because the robots aren’t better people. They’re better machines.
When technology changes, humans adapt. Like always. It usually happens in decades, not days.

last-horse-standing.nudge: And that’s just our take on jobs.

great-art-heist.title: The great art heist
great-art-heist.why: Why the people who pinch stuff aren’t always obvious.

blocks.x: The most valuable artwork you’ll ever own was painted by a child. That masterpiece with spiders for hands and awkward blobs as bodies.
It was splodged onto paper with great intent and proudly gets pinned on the fridge. Priceless.
Then they paint another one. And another. And another. Before you know it the walls are awash with spider-hand paintings of everyone they’ve met.
Yesterday’s masterpiece gets bumped for the next, day by kindergarten day. And much as you’d never say it out loud, they’re not nearly so special as the first one.
That’s the thing about art. It matters because of meaning. It has value because it’s unique.

So what happens when a robot can craft a hundred new artworks before you’ve finished your tea? Just set them to work, stealing from stuff they find online and squirting out pixels at the speed of prompt.
Hundreds of somethings. Nothing with meaning. Nothing to put on the fridge.
Artists have purpose. Robots have process. Only one of these things makes art.
The sixteen-year smile
There wasn’t so much AI in the early 16th century so people painted portraits with paint. Leonardo da Vinci was one such artist, renowned throughout Europe for his brushwork.
He was asked to paint the portrait of a merchant’s wife. So he did.

But the painting was never finished. Rather than hand it over, he kept it and tinkered for sixteen years. So the story wasn’t ‘artist paints a silk merchant’s missus’. It was ‘artist obsesses until the day he died’.

Then stories built on stories. The art was already famous. Then it was stolen. Story turned to legend and that enigmatic smile became one of the most widely shared images in the world. Posters, postcards, coffee mugs, T-shirts. Everyone knows the Mona Lisa. Few have seen the painting in the Louvre.
The artist obsessed over his artwork. The world climbed into his obsession.
And though the Mona Lisa is priceless, you can pick up a postcard on the streets of Paris for a euro. Same picture, slightly smaller, fewer brushstrokes.
One is an artwork, the other is not.

But pin your one special postcard on the fridge, and it turns into something new. You think, that’s the time we went to Paris. Remember the queue at the Louvre? I must confess, I wasn’t impressed by the smile.
The billionth reproduction is art again. Scarcity and meaning on the fridge.
Tech-faked scarcity goes bung
The talent of technology is easy reproduction. Infinite copies bouncing around the web. Nothing can be original until somebody signs it for real.

That was the thought behind NFTs. What if you could make digital art unique? Non-Fungible Tokens are digital receipts, like serial numbers for GIFs. Fungible is a mushroom-sounding word that means interchangeable. The goal was turning clicks into cash.

Problem is, it really didn’t work. Digital art is digital art regardless. Anyone who can right-click a mouse can easily make a copy. The NFT just proved that you’d paid for it. But pay for it people did.
For one crazy year in 2021 NFTs boomed to $25 billion before they crashed when people clocked that NFT Emperors weren’t wearing many clothes.
Manufactured scarcity never felt like art. And a pixelated punk or bored-looking ape is hard to claim as art on the best of days.
But the problem wasn’t the quality of the art. It was that proof of unique was irrelevant. You can’t just bolt on scarcity and cash a bigger cheque.
Video killed the radio star
Seems like every twenty years someone sets out to kill music.
MTV launched in 1981. They played that Buggles track as first cab off the rank. But video never killed the radio star. We all just changed channels and kept dancing.

Twenty years later, Napster started sharing songs for free. The labels panicked and rushed to court. Until Apple showed up charging 99c a song. Fans seemed happy to pay for the faves and the music kept on playing.
Twenty years on we flicked the switch again. MTV died of a streaming cold in 2025. And yes, they had the Buggles play it out.
But artists still made music and fans still followed their bands. Mostly. Streaming delivered the music. But something was missing in the feels.

From the moment streaming started, vinyl rose from the dead. Sales shot up year on year. An unexpected record boom driven by hungry fans. Turns out streams are fine to play the songs but humans like something they can touch.
Streaming couldn’t deliver what old-school records did. You need scarcity with your meaning to make it art.
Who’s stealing what and why?
If art lives in scarcity and meaning, the robots aren’t really a threat. Yes, they remix stuff they find online. But it’s math without meaning so there’s nobody home.
Art is born in the moment of its making. The money is in the means by which it’s shared. As we rush to judgement over digital theft, we miss the real robbery upstairs.
The studios, the platforms, the people who own the pipes. Who’s clipping the ticket on the artist’s work? That’s where the art heist happens.

You’d be very hard pressed to find a robot prepared to draw Mickey Mouse. That’s not because they object to drawing rodents. It’s just that Disney has the legal clout to sue. The artist drew the picture. The business locked it up. That’s scarcity manufactured by the law.
The robots run that racket in reverse. Eight billion humans shared work the robots play with. A handful of companies collect the subs. The art is in the making. The theft is in the pipes.
Because money is in the ownership of art. And when tech changes channels, the money moves with it.
Small artists suffer. Big artists sue. And it’s more about the money than the art.
But fans will always notice when the magic bit breaks. If you want to feel explosions you go to the movies. If you can’t touch a stream you head to a gig.
Because humans buying art are always chasing feels.
That new release on vinyl, that postcard from the Louvre, the spider-hand painting in your gallery on the fridge.
Technology just makes more stuff faster. Humans choose the meaning that makes it art.
Humans make art. Technology makes copies. The people who make money clip the ticket in the middle.

great-art-heist.nudge: And that’s just the fight about rights.

blocks.x: Kevin had a very clever puppy. It would fetch his slippers, answer the door and even scratch open the kibble to give itself a feed.
But when Kevin caught the puppy in the kitchen cooking eggs, it didn’t seem half so cute.
Agents are robots that do the work alone. They make their own decisions, solve their own problems and hammer their way through tedious stuff in their mission to get things done.
It’s all the same robots, just working by themselves. They can book stuff, they can buy stuff, they can build new toys online. They’re the holy grail of set and forget.
Just line up some rules, take your foot off the prompt and wait for the robot genius.
You can see why the corporates are buzzing ‘agentic’. More gets done, less time on tea breaks. It’s hard to see the downside.
Until somebody spots a puppy in the kitchen playing with gas.

deal-with-the-em-dash.title: What’s the deal with the em-dash?

blocks.x: Ever whipped through your robot draft to edit out the em-dash? It’s the fastest tell that a robot did your homework.
So why do the robots pepper them in? Best guess, it’s a quirk of training.
Every robot was taught by reading the world’s best writing. And ‘proper’ writers use them a lot. Dickens, Dickinson, Austen, you name them — all big fans of the afterthought punchline.

From there the models were tuned by humans. Turns out they like the casual clarity with an em-dash twist. Plus, robots don’t really write, they just glue stuff together — an em-dash is an easy dab of glue.
Put it all together and that’s how they got hooked.
Then the em-dash got robot-famous and people changed their minds.
It’s fashion, not punctuation. These days human writers dodge them to prove that their writing is real.
From good writing to popular writing to slop. And gone.
Poor little em-dash has suffered quite the ride.

robot-scientists.title: The robot scientists
robot-scientists.why: Why intelligence was never the bottleneck.

blocks.x: Remember all that paperwork in science class? Map out the method, record the results, and write it all up like we really need to show why the spud makes the clock work. Boring.

Most of us just wanted to burn stuff with the Bunsen and skewer the frog with a knife. But the boring bits of science are the bits that scientists care about. Record. Repeat. Record. Repeat. And make it seem credible by popping on a lab coat.
Can we not just get on with discovering stuff? Apparently not.

Because science is the industry that checks its own homework. It’s why we believe the stuff science says. It’s also why it’s painfully slow and it’s been that way since forever. But is that about to change? If the robots can cover the boring bits can we get to the science bits faster?
Mouldy magic
Remember Alexander Fleming? He’s the guy who gave us penicillin. Bit of a bumbler, not very tidy, left stuff on the shelf until it went mouldy. But that’s when he noticed something new.

Fleming realised that mould was attacking his experiment. It killed some bacteria growing in the dish. Fleming’s stroke of genius had nothing to do with laziness. It was spotting something weird and wondering why.
But that didn’t make Fleming an overnight success. Far from it. He made a discovery in an untidy lab, but it took ten years and a stack of experiments to turn his discovery into drugs.
Ideas, it seems, can come from anywhere. It’s just that proving the point through established science takes a lot more marathon than sprint.
What if the robots could change that?
Saving lives with soap
It wasn’t just Fleming who had to wait it out. History is packed with people who spotted a thing and then fought for years to earn their credibility.
One such genius was Ignaz Semmelweis. Along with having one of history’s best names, he made a simple discovery that still saves millions of lives.

Semmelweis was a doctor from back in the day, when they’d rush from patient to patient passing on germs as they went. An autopsy here, a baby to deliver there and very few stopped to wash their hands.
So he gave it a go. And it worked.
Mortality rates dropped dramatically. This bold new idea of doctors washing with soap could actually save lives. He proudly shared his findings and got laughed out of town.

He knew it worked, but he didn’t know why. So established doctors rejected the idea and nudged him onto the sidelines. Semmelweis wrote letter after letter calling other doctors murderers. That didn’t really help. They just had him committed. Never a great plan to suggest doctors are part of the problem.
Handwashing stayed optional for decades.
But what if genius is less about smarts and more about proof? What if all those write-ups were the point of it?
Fleming had a thought, but it took years to make it real. Semmelweis nailed a solution and the establishment washed their hands of him. Neither had the paperwork to prove it.
Wondering what this has to do with AI? Meet Demis Hassabis and his folding factory.
Nobel prizes for bots
Demis Hassabis is a video game designer. He started DeepMind, the British lab that crunched big numbers to show how robots spot patterns.
Tucked up at Google with infinite toys, he set out to find a new challenge. He asked himself, what if we use robots to prove a thing that science can’t land?
He picked protein folding.
Protein folding is one of the world’s biggest science puzzles. It’s also the key to the world’s best drugs.

That’s because proteins are the machinery of life. Every cell in your body runs on them. They carry oxygen, fight infection, build muscle and a whole lot more. You name it, proteins are into it. They’re important.

They start as a string of amino acids then fold into specific three-dimensional shapes to actually do their job. It’s the shape that matters. Get it wrong and it can lead to Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, Huntington’s. Get it right and you may have a cure.
The problem was predicting exactly how these proteins fold. It’s ridiculously complicated. There are more possible shapes than atoms in the universe.
Scientists had been working on it since the 60s. Thousands of biologists, fifty-odd years, building, testing, authenticating, one fold at a time.
Hassabis and his team briefed a robot. And they knocked it out in four.

AlphaFold studied shapes the humans had sorted and origamied the lot. It pulled out the patterns, tested the theories, double-checked its homework and spat out a massive stack of answers that pen-and-paper math never could.
They didn’t have a better insight. They had better tools.

In 2022 they released the predicted shapes of over 200 million proteins. Pretty much the known protein universe, free and publicly available, ready for testing in a lab. That’s a starting point for brand new drugs, nailed by a robot and recognised with a Nobel Prize.
Humans think. Robots grunt.
The difference between these stories isn’t the smarts of the scientists. It’s access to the proof that turns a brainwave into science.

Fleming found the answer, but couldn’t crack the question. Semmelweis spotted a pattern but couldn’t convince the room. Hassabis didn’t question the science, he used the robots to build on it and crunch impossible numbers. The science world read his proof and gave it a prize.

Genius is joining dots that no one else can see. The robot bit is digging through the other dots to prove it. The jury’s still out on whether a robot can crack an original idea. But once we’ve solved the clever bit, they’re ready to dive in and help.
It’s science without the boring bits. More time to play with frogs.
Genius, according to Edison, is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration. Robots can do the tedious bit, no sweat.

robot-scientists.nudge: And that’s just the science bit.

blocks.x: Digital tech loves the cool kid slogan: move fast and break things.
Harmless enough online. Way less cool in medicine.
Like that doctor in 2018 who was aiming to help kids at risk of HIV. He edited their genes to make them immune. Genius.
It’s hard to argue with his intent. He just did it before they were born.
It’s a fine line between a Nobel Prize and prison. He won the latter.
Ethics are only the norms of the day. They live in the gap between could we and should we. That’s the gap that’s shrinking.
Tech is already implanted into brains. We know how to edit our genes. “Perfect baby boy with lovely golden ringlets” is an ethics-shift away from real.
Less science fiction, more science horror.
As the tech keeps moving, it’s on us to hold the line.
We don’t mind doctors working miracles. We’d rather they didn’t play God.

second-order-of-things.title: The second order of things
second-order-of-things.why: Why the biggest revolution is still cooking.

blocks.x: Did you notice how everything is suddenly being sold with a handy side of AI? You’ve got AI fridges, AI lawnmowers, even an AI toothbrush that will tell you if you’re brushing on an angle.
You name it, someone’s shoved a robot in it. It’s just what happens when tech is hot.
We saw it in the Steam Age. Everything looked like an engine. And again with electricity when everything got a plug. And let’s not start on the dotcom boom. Makemybusinesscool.com
Every new tech shares the same basic story. Big hype and crazy inventions. Then a gradual descent into boring, attached to a monthly bill.

The bolt-on barrage is part of it. Trying new things is how tech gets better. Hand tools became mechanical tools. Mechanical tools got power. Power tools went cordless. And someone somewhere must be ramming some chips into cordless drills in the hope that AI can make more perfect holes.
But once the hype loses its heat, the tech will find its home.
And that’s when things start seriously changing.
Tech + tech = better tech
Second order innovation is more than adding a side of AI. It’s when two technologies meet and make something new. Think Uber.
Smartphones were the shiny new thing and maps had GPS. Put them together and taxis can’t keep up. Two ideas, one new tool. No one stops to ask how it works.
But Rome wasn’t built in a weekend. Often things take decades to evolve. Like the way they plugged the power into factories.

We all know the story of the factories and the farms. Impressive machines powered by steam could make more of everything faster. People chased jobs from the farms to the cities. And everyone marvelled at the output.
But steam-powered factories were noisy, hot and dangerous. Electric motors fixed all three. So they retired the stinky steam and bolted on some power.
And then the innovation stopped.

The challenge in most factories was still one source of grunt. A giant electric motor where the steam engine sat. Right across town we’d already invented much smaller motors that could do a better job. But it took over 30 years to bring them in.
Sometimes the obvious isn’t all that clear.

With small electric motors we could power different machines. So we cut the cord on the beast in the middle and set up factories to work like they should. Shifting the work to where it happens gave us assembly lines.
Factories got bigger, villages got smaller, electric lights gave us shift-work and power moved up the tree to the people flicking the switch.
Tech plus tech can take a generation. But it makes a bigger dent once it gets there.
Like shipping containers and global communications. Plug them together and it doesn’t matter where in the world your factory is. This gave us cheap, abundant everything and sweatshops.
If you’re wondering what drives this innovation, you just need to follow the money. Business doesn’t innovate for the fun of it. The goal is always more for less.
So how could AI mix and match to make the tills ring louder?
Sneakers while-u-wait
Let’s take two technologies, whack them together and listen for the sound of money. Here’s an idea with two we know: artificial intelligence and 3D printing.
What if you could pop into a shop and have a laser read your foot? Then the robot makes a pattern, especially for you. And zaps out the perfect shoes right there.

This is tech that’s just around the corner. The robots could walk all over it, the printing needs some work. If we tinker with that tech to print with multiple materials, you could get sneakers in your special size while you sip Diet Coke.
And there’s no need to worry, the robot knows that we buy shoes to fit in with our tribe. So every pair would show your stripes or give you a tick on the side.
But that’s stage one. What if this kit became small enough and cheap enough to keep it in your garage? And what if the shoes were just the start?
Broken a handle on your saucepan? No worries. Shove it in the replicator, get a new one just the same. ‘Earl Grey, hot’ was the Star Trek version. How long before we’re living science fiction?
And if that, then what?
We wouldn’t need shops, we wouldn’t need stock, we wouldn’t have great piles of waste. And those workers in far-flung factories could hang up their swipe cards for good.
And then what? Ask those farmers working in the factories. Or the horses that don’t pull carts. There are always winners and losers in the race of tech and money.
Healthy mirrors and flowing roads

The same approach can work for anything. Like a bathroom mirror that clocks your face on the daily? Plug in a couple of cameras and a data-crunching robot and maybe your mirror could track your health.
No checkups, no blood tests, no frantic quizzes with Dr Google. Just a daily review of vital signs, all while brushing your teeth.

And then there’s all that boring stuff like traffic. We already know about traffic light smarts. But what if all those lights were connected? Rather than leave a single light to manage what it sees, just tweak some lights on the other side of town and solve the bottleneck problem at source.
We couldn’t do that with switches and sensors. It’s a walk in the park for AI.
Ready for invisible robots?
This is how new tech works. We hype, we hope, we add a bit to everything. Then slowly it slides out of view.
We saw it with steam, we clicked through dotcom. And ‘electric’ spent years as a sales pitch for everything. These days we just buy a fridge.
Radio clicks in when we climb in the car, the internet is always-on. And we only ever think about power when we get the bill.
We’re right in the middle of the mush right now. AI is the answer to everything.
But sooner or later these thinking machines will settle in and find their mates. That’s when the big stuff starts to change. But slowly. Tech changes fast, societies shift in decades.
You’ll know the future’s here when you don’t even notice.
Every new tech starts out as hype. The big moves happen when your mum stops asking how it works.

second-order-of-things.nudge: And that’s just a peek at the future.

everything-old-is-new-again.title: Everything old is new again
everything-old-is-new-again.why: Why every generation thinks everything is new.

blocks.x: If you believe the very old books, a wealthy, warmongering king called Croesus once wandered up Mt Parnassus to seek advice from the Oracle of Delphi.

He was keen to confirm his plans for world domination. So he asked her what might happen if he took his troops to war. The Oracle, who was widely known to know everything, declared, “A great empire will fall.”
So Croesus, who heard what he wanted to hear, went galloping into battle and got roundly walloped by the Persians.
Turns out the Oracle never mentioned which empire. If only Croesus had a decent chatbot.
We love to fish for answers

Humans have always loved the idea of an all-knowing power that makes sense of the world. Some find it in religion. Others read the stars. And some build temples full of graphics cards that suck up human knowledge and spit it back in bite-sized chunks.
Same story, different tech.
In many ways these robots aren’t that different from the various answer books we’ve turned to before. We just trust them more because they were built by science.
This same old pattern of humans fishing for answers runs on repeat from the Ancient Greeks to Grok.
Tech changes how. Not who.
To really work out how to handle this tech, we need to know more about us. And the good news is that we haven’t really changed for over a quarter of a million years.
Just about everything good about humans started as a way to not die.
Trust was a short cut to avoid dodgy berries. Curiosity drove us to find new food so the tribe didn’t starve. We built a sense of belonging because loners mostly died.
It was brutal sharing the savannah with the lions.
Even our flaws were features out there. Laziness was a virtue, you eat less if you snooze. Deference was essential to fit in. And ego was the peacock move to find a better mate. Not much new in that.
That was all a while ago now, but it made us who we are. And we really haven’t changed that much.
If you peg human existence to a 24-hour day, we were dodging lions for 23 and the robots have been with us for a second. So the stuff that makes us human is pretty locked in.
We’re generous, we’re greedy, we’re open, we’re suspicious, we’re curious, we’re tribal, we love to fit in.
All this to say, people are people. And the tech hasn’t changed us. Yet.
New tricks old dogs
Even as technology changes, we know that humans don’t change much at all. We adopt the good stuff, adapt around the bad stuff and get grumpy when a password doesn’t work. It’s always been this way.
The printing press unsettled the churches until everyone settled down with the paper. The telephone didn’t invent connection. It just changed who we could talk to and when.
And when Steve Jobs made those phones touchable, it genuinely felt like magic. Now it only feels like magic when the kids put them down over dinner. Kids will be kids. Humans will be humans.
Technology doesn’t break the world. It just bends the ways we do what we do.
I think therefore I am
The reason AI feels different is the robots seem to be thinking.
We’re used to building tools that can give us better hands. But we worry about anything playing with our heads. Our brains are where we keep the good stuff.
That’s a line that’s uncomfortable to cross. But what if there wasn’t a line at all?
Us humans and these robots, we’re not nearly the same.
They’re super-impressive computers that crunch a billion thoughts in a second. We’re just human.
Fancy new oracle. Same old us.
It’s not a competition, because it can’t be. We’re too messy to lose.

Messy is the bit that makes us human. Messy is the bit that makes us great. We love when we know we shouldn’t. We laugh at the worst of jokes. And we stuff things up in a million ways that robots never can.

When some wine went bad we invented champagne. When the lab went mouldy we got drugs. When an actor fluffs their lines we get the best lines in the movies. So much of what we love was never in the plan.

Everyone knows a Croesus who only asks questions to hear their own answer. Everyone has a story of a stuff up that turned out good. Everyone who’s a human is at least a little bit broken. And that’s one thing the robots can never be.
They’re imperfect because they’re perfect. We’re perfect because we’re not.
New technology comes and goes and we all have the same old freak-out. And regardless of how clever the tech becomes, humans stay imperfectly human.

everything-old-is-new-again.nudge: And that’s why robots are just robots.

the-robot-under-your-bed.title: The robot under your bed
the-robot-under-your-bed.why: Why the robot stuff feels noisy until you play.

blocks.x: So here we all are, living with the robots. We love them for doing our homework, hate them for stealing our jobs and fear them because we’re not sure what comes next.
It’s a lot.
Are they clever? Yes. Are they dangerous? Possibly. Will they settle in, find their groove and end up all but invisible? Almost certainly.
Because once you get past their magic trick, you can start to see your robot for exactly what it is.
Not an oracle. That doesn’t work. Ask Croesus.
Not a mastermind. Just an over-confident parrot.
And it certainly wasn’t built to be a monster.
Just a brilliant machine that’s here to help.
Need a hand to crunch some numbers? Ask the robot. Need to bounce ideas? Ask the robot. Need a hundred different ways to sell a pair of socks?
Your robot will eat that up.
Because the thing the robots are best at is more. More answers, more options, a mountain of more. They lean on us to decide what’s good.
So the more robots we have in the world, the more we’ll need to value each other.
Our empathy. Our curiosity. Our judgement. Our mess.
Let the robots do what robots do best. And bring the bits that only you can.
Go drag that robot from under your bed. And play.
Don’t trust your robot
It might have all the answers, but it’s only ever guessing. And it smothers things in swagger so it’s hard to spot the join. Love it. But doubt it.
Don’t ignore your robot
Push buttons, ask questions, see what it can do. You can’t break it. It’s a robot. Tiny sparks of signal dancing in digital dust.
Don’t be a robot
Anyone can be a robot: questions in, answers out. Only you can bring the human to make those answers yours.

the-robot-under-your-bed.nudge: And that’s a beginning to end on.
